newsitem.title: ITALY: Castro arrives in Rome amid tight security.
newsitem.headline: Castro arrives in Rome amid tight security.

text.p: Cuban leader Fidel Castro, the long-awaited star of a U.N.-sponsored world food summit, arrived in Italy amid tight security on Saturday on a visit that may also include an historic meeting with the Pope.

Diplomatic sources said the 70-year-old communist president, one of the six summit vice-chairmen, was expected to address the meeting at the 1930s fascist-era building of the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) at around 1000 GMT.
Castro's arrival on the penultimate day of the summit came after days of speculation about his presence.
He had been due to deliver an address to the summit on Friday but failed to arrive in time. FAO officials said he had been unable to leave Havana due to bad weather.

Castro, dressed in military uniform, greeted a crowd of reporters at Rome's Fiumicino airport after his plane landed early on Saturday but ignored all questions as police ushered him quickly to a waiting car.
He is certain to use the summit stage to berate his ideological opponents in Washington and demand that a 34-year U.S.-imposed trade embargo against Cuba be lifted.
The U.N. General Assembly voted this week by its biggest majority in five years to lift the ban.

The Cuban leader's rare trip to Europe has been widely expected to involve a meeting with Pope John Paul. However no details have been released and Vatican officials have made clear they are waiting for Cuba to request an audience.
A meeting between the two men would cement improving relations between Cuba and the Roman Catholic Church and could pave the way for the Pontiff to visit Cuba next year.
The summit ends on Sunday when Castro is expected to take part in a final news conference in his role as a vice-chairman.

The crisis in eastern Zaire and plans to send an international force to the region have overshadowed the summit since delegates formally approved a plan of action and declaration on the opening day on Wednesday.

Castro's arrival was sure to take some of the media attention at the summit away from the crisis, which appeared to be easing slightly after tens of thousands of Hutu refugees began to return to Rwanda from Zaire on Friday.
Officials at the summit said they had already received 2,100 requests to interview Castro.
Several speakers called for the summit, which pledges to work towards halving global hunger within 20 years, to prevent similar crises.
"We have a solemn duty...to ensure that words are matched by actions on this critical issue," said Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, whose country holds the European Union presidency.

"We owe that duty to the hundreds of millions of men, women and children who are suffering from hunger and malnutrition and the many more who will suffer a similar fate in the future if we do not act effectively now," he added.
Britain's Overseas Development Minister Lynda Chalker reminded delegates that 20 years ago another United Nations conference had pledged to eliminate hunger.
"Bangladesh and Sahel were in the news then," she said. "Twenty two years on, we still have to remind ourselves of this commitment through the 1996 world food summit.
"Now Zaire and the Great Lakes region are dominating the headlines. We must not fail the world's poor and hungry again. Too many millions of lives are at stake."
